result:
Solution 3 is the most defensible of the three, though I could not fully verify that its value is the true exponent.

**Solution 1 is wrong.** It uses D(11/36 ‖ 5/12), which reverses the Stein direction. The type-I-constrained exponent is D(P⁰ ‖ P¹)-type, not D(P¹ ‖ P⁰)-type. It also falls below an achievable value. Sending a Slepian–Wolf hash of X on a fraction q = 0.1837 of the positions (rate q·h₂(1/3) = R) and using only Y elsewhere gives exponent q·D(1/3 ‖ 1/9) ≈ 0.0462 > 0.0380.

**Solution 2 is unjustified.** It asserts E = D(5/12 ‖ 1/4) without a derivation. The identity D(5/12 ‖ 1/4) = (1/6)log₂3 − R does hold exactly, but that does not establish the exponent.

**Solution 3 checks out as the optimized quantize-and-bin value.**
- The rate matches: R = I(U;X|Y) for U = X ⊕ Bern(1/4).
- Minimizing ¾D(α‖1/9) + ¼D(γ‖1/9) subject to 3α − γ = 2/3 gives 567α² − 114α − 5 = 0, so α = 5/21 and γ = 1/21. I verified 64αγ = (1−α)(1−γ).
- Expanding the resulting KL terms gives exactly 1/3 + (5/12)log₂5 − log₂(7/3) ≈ 0.0784.

The problem's choice of R to match the crossover 1/4 (which gives P(Y=1) = 5/12 under H₀) suggests the intended optimal test channel is this BSC(1/4). I did not prove that no other auxiliary U or scheme beats 0.0784, so the exact optimality of this value remains unconfirmed.

CHOICE: 3
